title: Git Flow
description: Understand the Git Flow branching model with its develop, feature, release, hotfix, and support branches.

data.text: Git Flow is a branching model created by Vincent Driessen that defines a strict set of long-lived branches with well-defined purposes. It is designed for projects with scheduled releases and is the most formally structured of the common Git workflows.

data.title: Git Flow branches
items: **main** — Production-ready code. Every commit on main is a release.
**develop** — Integration branch for features. The next release is branched from here.
**feature/** — Branched from develop. Merged back into develop when complete.
**release/** — Branched from develop. Bug fixes only. Merged into both main and develop.
**hotfix/** — Branched from main. Urgent production fixes. Merged into both main and develop.

data.title: Git Flow command workflow
data.code:
# Initialize Git Flow
git flow init -d

# Start a feature branch
git flow feature start add-user-auth

# Finish the feature (merges into develop)
git flow feature finish add-user-auth

# Start a release branch
git flow release start v1.2.0

# Finish the release (merges into main and develop)
git flow release finish v1.2.0

# Hotfix for production
git flow hotfix start v1.2.1

git flow hotfix finish v1.2.1

data.text: A release branch is created from develop when the team decides the next release is feature-complete. Only bug fixes go into the release branch. When it is ready, it is merged into main (tagged as a release) and back into develop (to include the fixes).

data.title: Release branches isolate stabilization
data.text: The release branch lets the team stabilize for production while developers continue working on the next release in develop. This is the key insight of Git Flow.

Hotfix branches are branched directly from main, allowing you to fix production issues without including in-progress features from develop. The fix is merged back into both main and develop when complete.

items: Projects with regular, scheduled releases (e.g., every 2 weeks)
Teams that need a clear stabilization period before release
Products with a production support model
Organizations that value explicit process and audit trails
Continuous deployment teams shipping multiple times per day
SaaS products with no traditional release boundary
Small teams that prefer minimal ceremony
Open-source projects with a single maintainer

items.question: Is git-flow a Git command?
items.answer: Yes. git flow is an extension to Git providing commands like git flow feature start. Install it separately (brew install git-flow-avh on macOS, apt install git-flow on Ubuntu).

items.question: Do I need the git-flow extension?
items.answer: No. You can follow the Git Flow model using standard Git commands. The extension just provides convenient wrappers for the common operations.

items.question: How does Git Flow handle version tags?
items.answer: Tags are applied to main when a release branch is finished. The naming convention is usually vX.Y.Z matching your versioning scheme.

items.question: Can I use Git Flow with trunk-based development?
items.answer: They are different models. Git Flow encourages long-lived branches; trunk-based encourages short-lived branches. Mixing them defeats the purpose of both.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Git Flow defines five branch types with strict purposes
develop is the integration branch; main contains only releases
Release branches isolate stabilization from active development
Hotfixes branch from main for urgent production issues
Git Flow is ideal for scheduled releases but overkill for CD teams
